quests.correctSentence: Thank you for your proposal. While we appreciate the offer, we believe the terms could be more favorable to both parties.
quests.contrastSentence: Thank you for your proposal. Because we appreciate the offer, we believe the terms could be more favorable to both parties.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'While' introduces a polite contrast in formal writing: while we appreciate it, we believe it could improve. This softens the pushback that follows.
quests.nativeTip: The email politely contrasts appreciation with a request for better terms.

quests.correctSentence: Should you be willing to reconsider the pricing, we would be glad to move forward immediately.
quests.contrastSentence: Would you be willing to reconsider the pricing, we would be glad to move forward immediately.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should you be willing' is the formal inverted first-conditional opener, common in negotiation emails to sound polished and non-confrontational.
quests.nativeTip: This formal opening replaces 'if you were willing' with an inverted structure.

quests.correctSentence: — Can we meet halfway on this? — I think that would be a reasonable compromise for everyone involved.
quests.contrastSentence: — Can we meet halfway on this? — I think that will be a reasonable compromise for everyone involved.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would' expresses a tentative, hypothetical suggestion in negotiation: that would be reasonable, softer than a direct 'will'.
quests.nativeTip: This is a hypothetical compromise being proposed, not yet agreed.

quests.correctSentence: As you can see from the chart, sales have increased significantly over the past quarter.
quests.contrastSentence: As you can see from the chart, sales increased significantly over the past quarter.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect fits a change over an ongoing period connected to now: have increased over the past quarter, a very common structure in presentations.
quests.nativeTip: The chart shows a change connected to right now, over an unfinished period ('this quarter').

quests.correctSentence: This approach is far more effective than the one we used last year.
quests.contrastSentence: This approach is far most effective than the one we used last year.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Far more' intensifies a comparative adjective: far more effective. 'Far most' isn't correct English; intensifiers like 'far' only pair with comparatives.
quests.nativeTip: 'Far' intensifies a comparative, not a superlative.

quests.correctSentence: — Any questions so far? — Just one: does this strategy also apply to smaller teams?
quests.contrastSentence: — Any questions so far? — Just one: is this strategy also apply to smaller teams?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Does this strategy apply' asks about general applicability using simple present, appropriate for a question about how something generally works.
quests.nativeTip: This asks about a general applicability, not a one-time future event.

quests.correctSentence: I understand you're frustrated that your order hasn't arrived yet.
quests.contrastSentence: I understand you're frustrated that your order didn't arrived yet.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Yet' pairs with present perfect negative: hasn't arrived yet, connecting the missing delivery to the present moment of the complaint.
quests.nativeTip: The word 'yet' at the end is a strong signal for this specific tense.

quests.correctSentence: Had we been notified sooner, we would have resolved this before it became a problem.
quests.contrastSentence: Had we been notified sooner, we will have resolved this before it became a problem.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had we been notified' is an inverted third conditional, so the result clause needs 'would have': we would have resolved this.
quests.nativeTip: This inverted structure needs its matching third-conditional result.

quests.correctSentence: — The representative told me it would be fixed by Friday. — I'm sorry that that didn't happen; let me personally look into it.
quests.contrastSentence: — The representative told me it would be fixed by Friday. — I'm sorry for that didn't happen; let me personally look into it.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Sorry that' introduces a full clause explaining the apology's cause: sorry that it didn't happen, distinct from 'sorry for/about' plus a noun.
quests.nativeTip: This word introduces the reason for the apology as a full clause.

quests.correctSentence: By the time we reached the gate, the flight had already departed.
quests.contrastSentence: By the time we reached the gate, the flight has already departed.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'By the time' signals past perfect: the flight had departed before we arrived, one past event completed before another.
quests.nativeTip: One past event finished before another past event, our arrival at the gate.

quests.correctSentence: She must have missed the announcement; she was wearing headphones the whole time.
quests.contrastSentence: She might have missed the announcement; she was wearing headphones the whole time.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Must have' draws a strong, near-certain conclusion from the evidence: she must have missed it, given the headphones.
quests.nativeTip: The headphones make this conclusion almost certain.

quests.correctSentence: — Do you know what happened to our luggage? — I'm not sure, but it might still be on the previous flight.
quests.contrastSentence: — Do you know what happened to our luggage? — I'm not sure, but it must still be on the previous flight.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Might' expresses a real but uncertain possibility, fitting the speaker's own admission of not being sure.
quests.nativeTip: The speaker is genuinely uncertain, just guessing at a possibility.

quests.correctSentence: Looking back, I wish I had taken that job offer when I had the chance.
quests.contrastSentence: Looking back, I wish I have taken that job offer when I had the chance.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Wish I had taken' expresses regret about a past action, using past perfect after 'wish', the same backshift pattern as third conditional if-clauses.
quests.nativeTip: 'Wish' about the past needs the same backshifted form as third conditional.

quests.correctSentence: I have been thinking about this decision for weeks, and I still don't have an answer.
quests.contrastSentence: I has been thinking about this decision for weeks, and I still don't have an answer.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I' takes 'have' in present perfect continuous: have been thinking, emphasizing an ongoing mental process up to now.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'I' needs the matching present perfect continuous helper verb.

quests.correctSentence: — Any regrets about the move? — If I had known how hard it would be, I might have reconsidered.
quests.contrastSentence: — Any regrets about the move? — If I have known how hard it would be, I might have reconsidered.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'If I had known' is a third conditional if-clause, expressing an unreal past situation, paired here with 'might have reconsidered'.
quests.nativeTip: This is a hypothetical about a past situation that cannot be changed now.

quests.correctSentence: The data was collected over a six-month period.
quests.contrastSentence: The data is collected over a six-month period.
quests.ruleExplanation: In this common usage, 'data' is treated as a singular collective subject: the data was collected, describing a completed past process.
quests.nativeTip: The subject 'data' is treated as singular in this common usage, and the collection finished in the past.

quests.correctSentence: These findings, which were presented at the conference, support our initial hypothesis.
quests.contrastSentence: These findings, that were presented at the conference, support our initial hypothesis.
quests.ruleExplanation: Commas signal a non-defining relative clause, which requires 'which', never 'that': the findings, which were presented, support the hypothesis.
quests.nativeTip: The comma before and after this clause signals extra, non-essential information.

quests.correctSentence: — How reliable is this data? — It can't be considered fully reliable, given the small sample size.
quests.contrastSentence: — How reliable is this data? — It must be considered fully reliable, given the small sample size.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Can't' expresses a strong negative conclusion based on evidence: can't be considered reliable, given the small sample size mentioned.
quests.nativeTip: The small sample size rules out full reliability.

quests.correctSentence: If you take this role, you will be leading a team of twelve by next quarter.
quests.contrastSentence: If you take this role, you would be leading a team of twelve by next quarter.
quests.ruleExplanation: First conditional describes a realistic future outcome: if you take the role, you will be leading a team, a genuine likely result.
quests.nativeTip: This is a real, likely outcome of a real future possibility.

quests.correctSentence: I've been considering you for this position for a while now.
quests.contrastSentence: I've was considering you for this position for a while now.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I've been considering' completes present perfect continuous, showing an ongoing thought process leading up to this conversation.
quests.nativeTip: This completes the present perfect continuous form after 've.

quests.correctSentence: — What would change day to day? — You would report directly to me instead of your current manager.
quests.contrastSentence: — What would change day to day? — You will report directly to me instead of your current manager.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Would' fits this hypothetical description of a not-yet-official arrangement: you would report to me, matching the question's own hypothetical tone.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a hypothetical arrangement being discussed, not yet official.

quests.correctSentence: In some cultures, it is considered impolite to refuse an invitation directly.
quests.contrastSentence: In some cultures, it was considered impolite to refuse an invitation directly.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present simple passive fits general truths about customs: it is considered impolite, a fact that holds generally, not just once.
quests.nativeTip: This is a general truth about cultural norms, true in general, not a one-time event.

quests.correctSentence: If you don't mind me asking, how is this typically handled in your office?
quests.contrastSentence: Should you don't mind me asking, how is this typically handled in your office?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'If you don't mind me asking' is a fixed polite opener for a possibly sensitive question, useful across cultural and professional contexts.
quests.nativeTip: This is a polite, cautious way of introducing a potentially sensitive question.

quests.correctSentence: — How should I address my new manager? — It's usually best to stay formal until they suggest otherwise.
quests.contrastSentence: — How should I address my new manager? — It's usually best staying formal until they suggest otherwise.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Best to stay' takes the infinitive: it's best to stay formal, a natural structure for giving cautious cross-cultural advice.
quests.nativeTip: 'Best' pairs with the infinitive form of the following verb here.

quests.correctSentence: Had the results had been shared earlier, the team could have adjusted the strategy in time.
quests.contrastSentence: Have the results had been shared earlier, the team could have adjusted the strategy in time.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had the results been shared' is an inverted third conditional, dropping 'if' entirely, common in formal analysis and reports.
quests.nativeTip: This drops 'if' and inverts the auxiliary and subject for a formal third conditional.

quests.correctSentence: The proposal, which took months to prepare, was ultimately rejected by the board.
quests.contrastSentence: The proposal, that took months to prepare, was ultimately rejected by the board.
quests.ruleExplanation: Non-defining relative clauses require 'which', never 'that', signaled here by the surrounding commas.
quests.nativeTip: Commas around this clause signal extra, non-essential information about the proposal.

quests.correctSentence: — What's the update? — We're still waiting to hear whether the client has approved the budget.
quests.contrastSentence: — What's the update? — We're still waiting to hear that the client has approved the budget.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whether' introduces this indirect yes/no question as a noun clause: waiting to hear whether they approved it, reviewing this structure from Stage 7.
quests.nativeTip: This introduces an indirect yes/no question about approval.

quests.correctSentence: When I started this course, I could barely form a sentence in English.
quests.contrastSentence: When I started this course, I can barely form a sentence in English.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Could' expresses general past ability: could barely form a sentence, describing a skill level that has since clearly changed, reviewing a structure from very early in this course.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a general past ability, all the way back at the beginning of the journey.

quests.correctSentence: Had I known then how far I would come, I might have believed it sooner.
quests.contrastSentence: Have I known then how far I would come, I might have believed it sooner.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had I known' is an inverted third conditional, reflecting on a hypothetical past, drawing together the inversion and conditional skills built across the later stages of this course.
quests.nativeTip: This inverted structure looks back on the entire journey from Level 1 to now.

quests.correctSentence: Looking ahead, I know that fluency is built one conversation at a time, and I'm ready for what comes next.
quests.contrastSentence: Looking ahead, I know that fluency was built one conversation at a time, and I'm ready for what comes next.
quests.ruleExplanation: This final answer returns to present simple passive, the simplest possible structure, echoing the very first grammar point of this entire 200-level journey: fluency is built one conversation at a time.
quests.nativeTip: This is a general, lasting truth, the same simple structure practiced back at Level 1, now carrying the weight of everything learned since.
